meta.title: Cost flows and the manufacturing statements
meta.summary: How manufacturing costs flow from materials through work in process and finished goods to cost of goods sold, the schedule of cost of goods manufactured, the manufacturer's income statement, the journal entries, and three meanings of product cost.

videos.title: How costs flow through a factory
videos.take: Manufacturing costs flow from materials to work in process, finished goods and cost of goods sold

scenes.say: Manufacturing costs move through the accounts the same way trailers move through the factory. Follow the flow.

scenes.heading: The cost flow
scenes.say: Materials are bought into materials inventory. When they're used, their cost moves into work in process, joined by direct labor and manufacturing overhead. When trailers are finished, their cost moves to finished goods. When they're sold, it becomes cost of goods sold.
Every inventory account follows the same equation: beginning balance, plus what comes in, minus what goes out, equals the ending balance. Know three numbers and you can find the fourth.

scenes.heading: Work-in-process, October
scenes.say: Prairie Gate's work in process started October with $110,000. It received $196,000 of materials, $88,000 of direct labor and $132,000 of overhead. $400,000 of trailers were finished and moved out, leaving $126,000.

sub: Inventoriable costs stay on the balance sheet
scenes.say: The key idea: inventoriable costs follow the product. They only reach the income statement when the trailer is sold.

scenes.q: Finished goods began at $64,000; $400,000 was completed; ending is $58,000. What is cost of goods sold?
scenes.say: Quick check. Finished goods began at sixty-four thousand, four hundred thousand was completed, and the ending balance is fifty-eight thousand. What's cost of goods sold? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Direct materials used
videos.take: Direct materials used equals beginning materials plus purchases minus ending materials

scenes.say: Purchases aren't the same as materials used. The difference sits in the storeroom.

scenes.heading: Prairie Gate, October
scenes.say: Prairie Gate began October with $70,000 of steel, axles and tires. It bought $210,000 more, so $280,000 was available. $84,000 was still in the storeroom at month-end, so $196,000 was used in production.
If Prairie Gate stocks up on steel before a price increase, purchases jump, but materials used, and product cost, don't.
Some materials are too small to trace, like welding wire and grease. These indirect materials go to manufacturing overhead, not direct materials.

sub: from the storeroom to a job
scenes.say: In practice, a materials requisition records each issue from the storeroom to a specific trailer, which is how job costing will trace materials in Lecture 4.

scenes.q: Beginning materials $30,000, purchases $95,000, ending $25,000. Materials used?
scenes.say: Quick check. Beginning materials thirty thousand, purchases ninety-five thousand, ending twenty-five thousand. What was used? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Cost of goods manufactured
videos.take: COGM adds this period's manufacturing costs to beginning WIP and subtracts ending WIP

scenes.say: The schedule of cost of goods manufactured shows the cost of everything finished this period. Let's build it.

scenes.heading: Manufacturing costs incurred, October
scenes.say: In October, Prairie Gate used $196,000 of direct materials and incurred $88,000 of direct labor and $132,000 of overhead: $416,000 of manufacturing costs.

scenes.heading: Schedule of cost of goods manufactured
scenes.say: Add the $110,000 of trailers that were partly built at the start, for $526,000 to account for. Subtract the $126,000 still in process at month-end. Cost of goods manufactured, the cost of trailers finished in October, is $400,000.
Notice the difference. Prairie Gate spent $416,000 this month but finished $400,000 of trailers, because work in process grew.
The schedule is just the work-in-process T-account, written out as a report.

scenes.q: Costs incurred $300,000, beginning WIP $40,000, ending WIP $55,000. COGM?
scenes.say: Quick check. Costs incurred three hundred thousand, beginning work in process forty thousand, ending fifty-five thousand. What's cost of goods manufactured? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The manufacturer's income statement
videos.take: COGS equals beginning finished goods plus COGM minus ending finished goods

scenes.say: Cost of goods manufactured feeds the income statement through finished goods. Here's the last step.

scenes.heading: Cost of goods sold, October
scenes.say: Prairie Gate began with $64,000 of finished trailers on the lot. Add the $400,000 manufactured, for $464,000 available for sale. $58,000 of trailers remain unsold, so cost of goods sold is $406,000.

scenes.heading: Income statement, October
scenes.say: Revenues were $560,000. Less cost of goods sold, gross margin is $154,000. Less $96,000 of period costs for marketing, distribution and administration, operating income is $58,000.

scenes.heading: Merchandiser vs manufacturer
scenes.say: A merchandiser's statement looks the same, except purchases take the place of cost of goods manufactured, and it has one inventory instead of three.
Period costs skip the inventory accounts entirely and go straight to the income statement.

scenes.q: Revenue $800,000, COGS $520,000, period costs $190,000. Operating income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Revenue eight hundred thousand, cost of goods sold five twenty, period costs one ninety. Operating income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Journal entries for cost flows
videos.take: Each step of the flow is a journal entry moving cost from one account to the next

scenes.say: Every arrow in the cost flow is a journal entry. Here are the main ones for October.

scenes.heading: Use materials and labor
scenes.say: Issuing direct materials debits work in process and credits materials: $196,000. Direct labor debits work in process and credits wages payable: $88,000.

scenes.heading: Overhead
scenes.say: Actual overhead costs, like utilities and depreciation, are first collected in manufacturing overhead control. Then they're moved into work in process. In Lecture 5 you'll see that companies usually apply overhead using a predetermined rate instead.

scenes.heading: Finish and sell
scenes.say: Completed trailers move from work in process to finished goods: $400,000. Trailers sold move from finished goods to cost of goods sold: $406,000. A separate entry records the revenue.

sub: The general ledger total, backed by
subsidiary ledgers by job or material
scenes.say: The word control means a general ledger account backed by a subsidiary ledger: individual job cost records behind work in process, for example.
Quick check. Which entry records trailers completed? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Cost moves out of work in process into finished goods.

videos.title: Three meanings of product cost
videos.take: Product cost differs for pricing, government contracting and external reporting

scenes.say: What did a trailer cost? The answer depends on why you're asking. Here are three definitions of product cost.

scenes.heading: Three product costs
scenes.say: For pricing and product-mix decisions, product cost includes the whole value chain, from design to customer service. For a government cost-plus contract, it includes only the costs the contract allows. For the financial statements, it includes only manufacturing costs.

scenes.heading: Trailer #418, three ways
scenes.say: Trailer four-eighteen's GAAP inventory cost is $11,480. Add design, marketing, delivery and expected warranty costs, and its full value-chain cost is $13,580. Pricing it at $13,000 would look profitable on the GAAP number, but it isn't.
Suppose Lyon County buys six utility trailers on a cost-plus-eight-percent contract. The contract decides which costs count, so the accounting must follow it, not GAAP.
It's the theme of the course again: different costs for different purposes. Always ask what the cost is for.

scenes.q: Which product cost should Karen use to set the long-run price of a trailer model?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which product cost should Karen use for a long-run price? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. In the long run, prices must cover every cost in the value chain.

case: Prairie Gate's November data: beginning DM $84,000, purchases $190,000, ending DM $76,000; direct labor $92,000; manufacturing overhead $138,000; beginning WIP $126,000, ending WIP $98,000; beginning FG $58,000, ending FG $71,000; revenue $640,000; marketing and admin $101,000. Karen asks why operating income rose even though fewer trailers were finished than she expected.
Compute DM used, COGM and COGS.

What does Karen's question reveal about the timing of costs?

DM used 198,000; costs incurred 428,000; COGM 456,000; COGS 443,000; gross margin 197,000; OI 96,000. WIP fell, so trailers started in October were finished in November. Costs reach income only when trailers are sold, so production and sales timing drive reported income.
exam: Explain the flow of manufacturing costs through the accounts, from purchase to sale.
Materials purchased (materials inventory) → used (WIP) with DL and MOH → completed (FG) → sold (COGS). Each move is a journal entry; balances follow beginning + in − out = ending.
Given DM used $180,000, DL $70,000, MOH $105,000, beginning WIP $45,000, ending WIP $60,000, beginning FG $30,000, ending FG $25,000, compute COGM and COGS.
outcomes: Trace costs through the manufacturing accounts

take: COGM = beginning WIP + costs incurred − ending WIP
COGS = beginning FG + COGM − ending FG
Each arrow in the flow is a journal entry
Product cost depends on the purpose
